author: ACG
title: CITIZENSHIP LAWS IN IRELAND
content:
The coalition government in the south of Ireland is proposing to change the rules surrounding citizenship. At the moment it takes 5 years to become a naturalised citizen. The intention of Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration James O’Callaghan, is that it will require 8 years. In addition, you can’t have had welfare payments in the last 2 years of that period. Plus you need to show you have a certain level of ability in Irish or English. Let’s look at what is driving these revisions.




The change seems to come out of nowhere. One of  O’Callaghan’s explicitly declared reasons for the modification of the law is a technical one. He says that Ireland is an outlier in European Union (EU) terms and should be brought into line with EU norms. He cited Germany as an example of a country that requires an 8 year wait. The trouble is, this is just factually not true. Germany actually reduced its requirements from 8 to 5 years in 2024 (https://www.bmi.bund.de/SharedDocs/kurzmeldungen/EN/2024/06/mod-staatsangehoerigkeitsrecht.html).




 In reality, there are a variety of conditions across the EU. Twelve of the 27 member states have a standard residence requirement of five years for naturalisation, according to a report published in 2025 by the Robert Schuman Centre for Advanced Studies (https://globalcit.eu/new-globalcit-study-compares-conditions-for-citizenship-acquisition-by-immigrants-and-their-descendants/).




Another argument employed was that the changes “…seek to ensure that citizenship reflects a demonstrated, durable connection to Ireland, knowledge of the state and its institutions, and a sustained commitment to participation in Irish society” (Dublin People, 7/10/26). Even if you accepted the desirability of these qualities, how can such vague and subjective things be adequately measured? We are expected to believe that 5 years would not prove a durable connection or a commitment to participation in “Irish society” but 8 years has magically achieved that? It is really just an arbitrary number.




There is clearly more at work behind the scenes. One possible reason for the adjustment is the current Taoiseach/Leader of the Government Michael Martin is seen as vulnerable on his Right flank and O’Callaghan senses an opportunity to look tough as part of a future bid to depose him. So in that aspect, socially vulnerable sectors of society are being used as pawns in an elite power game.




Besides the personally ambitious dimension, there’s also the ideological one of using immigrants as a red herring or scapegoat for failures of the system. By putting pressure on relative newcomers, longer term residents and those born on the island are expected to divert attention towards those supposedly less worthy than themselves. It’s not big business, landlords and their friends in government who are to blame for the housing crisis, energy prices or the general cost of living. It’s Maria the cleaner and Pedro the kitchen hand who have been in Ireland ‘too long’ and need to be discouraged from staying. In other words, classic divide-and-rule.




The new amendments clearly have a class element to them. Imagine you have saved some money and decide to embark on a long journey to start a new life. You secure a job undertaking physical labour, probably one not many of the locals want to do. You work hard for 5 or 6 years. Then you have an accident or develop a disability. Or maybe you lose the job because a tanker is bottle-necked in a canal overseas or a madman running a rogue state starts a war against a small oil rich nation causing delays in supply lines, an increase in prices and lay offs. Or perhaps AI and the development of robots means employers are less reliant on human labour. Any number of reasons beyond your control could cause you difficulty. You’ve paid taxes. You apply for welfare support. Great, don’t expect citizenship now. It’s your own fault, you foreign parasite.




A common phenomenon is one where as an immigrant you take a job that makes it difficult for you socially. Its not uncommon to have a graveyard shift working alone or with fellow immigrants. Likewise you might have to live with people from a similar background. That’s either due to discrimination or lack of finances to take up other options. In reality, due to the cost of living you may actually have to take-on another job as well, just to get ahead. Somehow in such a schedule you have to find time for sleep and to become highly articulate in another language. Even if you can spare an hour to study, who will pay for quality lessons? Well, that’s up to you.




In case the above seems too anecdotal, there are specific categories of people who are already in the firing line due to the changes. Ukrainians who have been in Ireland due to the full scale invasion of the country in 2022 and are covered by the Temporary Protection Directive, will not be allowed to put the time they’ve already spent on the island towards a citizenship application. Another case concerns over a hundred Palestinian students who have had their application for university places denied and will not be permitted to have their cases reviewed. So, with people from war-torn regions getting treated like disposable items, the conditions for others are likely to get harder too.













There are clearly tough times ahead in Ireland. It’s possible some as yet unforseen counter-measure may negate or cancel the government’s new moves. It seems unlikely. Even if O’Callaghan and his faction no longer continue to have the upper hand in implementing more severe measures, this stuff is not just the vanity project of an individual leader-manque. The macro-level landscape is one dominated by capitalism and the nation-state as organising actors. This is based on imaginary boundaries, of in/out dichotomies, extreme hierarchies and private or state ownership and control of resources in a particular geographical area.This combination results in the harsh absurdities ordinary working people suffer from.




Given the arbitrary nature of the system, its tempting to make moral or rational arguments that oppose the basis and method by which citizenship is or isn’t granted.Take for example the way the island was partitioned in the 1920s’ along (literally) lines that were not favoured by the majority and still aren’t. Perhaps such facts could be used to as a starting point for a discussion on the wider question of the nation-state.




Likewise, statistical material showing the economic reliance the system has upon those not born on the island, can be useful. For example, the OECD International Migration Outlook 2025 highlights that 43% of Doctors in Ireland qualified elsewhere, compared with an OECD average of 20% and 52% of nurses, more than anywhere else they surveyed  (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/international-migration-outlook-2025_ae26c893-en/full-report/international-migration-of-health-professionals-to-oecd-countries_fea88ae4.html).). It’s true in this case the numbers include a few born in Ireland who may have studied elsewhere. However, that just shows the relative generosity of those places.




Taking another crucial sector, approximately 25% of workers in the construction industry are not considered Irish according to the Central Office of Statistics (CSO) (https://www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/ep/p-biilmss/businessinireland2025-labourmarketandsocialsustainability/laboursupply/). One of the most notable areas where non-Irish workers contribute is in hospitality, restaurants and hotels. According to the CSO, they comprise 46% of the workforce (https://www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/ep/p-eaads/earningsanalysisusingadministrativedatasources2025/nationality/).




So even a cursory look at the economy reveals meaningful contributions to society as a whole by incoming workers. Of course, not everybody is statistically inclined or will be convinced by any amount of numbers you chuck at them. Its certainly not being suggested here that those running things at the top will change course significantly, once they know these facts. They already know them.




Having moral, historical, logical and statistical arguments can form an element of whats required to oppose the naturalisation changes. However, that’s not enough unless there’s also practical organising on our streets, in workplaces and neighbourhoods. There have already been some small, poorly attended street demonstrations in Dublin, for example. It’s a start, but a lot more needs to be done.




The task ahead is to forge links between all workers, regardless of origin and nationality. Building networks that transcend differences of language, birth, age, ability etc and focusing on our common condition as participants in an economic and political arrangement that is kicking us all. This could involve existing organisations when and where they are useful, or more likely, building them from scratch. It won’t be easy but as citizens of the world, its something we have to attempt. As the Nineteenth Century Irish radical James Fintan Lalor put it -“ Remember this-that somewhere and somehow, and by somebody, a beginning must be made”.




B.

author: Erica Malatesta
title: Scotland: Anti-Data Centre Movement Gathers Momentum
content:
“Every time you ask ChatGPT a question, read a Google summary or make an online bank payment, a data centre is working behind the scenes. Now Scotland is part of a global race to build many more of them – on a massive scale. The explosion in artificial intelligence (AI) over the past few years has seen tech firms scrambling to build new “hyperscale” data centres, including some which would rank among the biggest in the world. Plans are in place to build at least 23 giant AI-powered data centres” (

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6qxv55882z1o

).




AI has insinuated itself into all areas of life and society. For example in education, it has managed to secure huge contracts with universities and schools, leading to the forcing of AI on teachers and students.




AI is controlled by Big Tech capitalists and by heads of state. It hopes to create huge dividends for shareholders and profits for its owners while claiming to be good for society.




AI has not stopped war. It is developing techniques to destroy cities and kill people remotely. It has not created better working conditions, the end of unemployment, and an improvement in living standards. It has done the opposite. It has not led to a solution to climate change. In fact, the mass development of data centres will accelerate climate change. It has not led to social progress. In fact, the plutocrats are increasingly taking over and controlling the media, political and social power and moving towards increasingly more authoritarian forms of rule, in order to preserve and regenerate a failing capitalism.




The uprising against data centres is therefore also a revolt against AI and against a system that puts profits before people and the planet.




Where are the Data Centres




The map, produce by the Action for the Protection of Rural Scotland (APRS), shows the extent of proposed data centres (

https://aprs.scot/data-centres-campaign/

).




Some of the biggest ones planned are:




Chapel Stile Data Centre (Dumfriesshire)




The Ferret, well-known for its hard-hitting, independent and thoroughly-researched journalism says:




“CX Tech Limited has lodged plans for a 1,000 megawatt (MW) data centre at the site of the former Chapelcross nuclear plant in Dumfriesshire, which could benefit from up to £23m in taxpayer support. Company records show CX Tech’s controlling shareholder is Wpgss Limited, which is owned by property mogul and Tory treasurer Graham Edwards through a holding company registered in the British Virgin Islands (BVI) – a notorious tax and secrecy haven.” (https://www.theferret.scot/scotland-data-centre-graham-edwards/)




Auchertool: Fife




The site would span 60 hectares, about the size of 84 football pitches. It would be bigger than the village itself, completely transforming the life of the village. People are concerned at the noise and pollution, the impact on health and the sheer size of the development. As one villager said: “The village will be left in the shadows of the data centre. It’s huge. It is like having a tower block laid on its side plonked in the middle of the countryside.” (https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cddle43jr1go)




‘Green’ Data Centres




The applications for the big data centres are claiming to be ‘green’. This way they can be considered to be part of “National Development 12”. It is up to the planning authority to interpret and apply the guidelines. According to Action for the Protection of Rural Scotland: “We believe that there will be serious unintended consequences of this policy until a strict definition of a green data centre is established, combined with an overall limit to the amount of energy that Scotland intends to divert to data centres. We have looked at data centres in development around Scotland and have seen that, in many planning application documents, or pre-application consultations, they are describing themselves as ‘green’ data centres. This can range from claiming to be green because they have solar panels on the roof to claiming the fact they use grid electricity in Scotland makes them green, some mention using waste heat in heat networks.”




The Ferret

 has found that data centre companies themselves are working closely with government to define ‘green’. “The Ferret has found that in the months leading up to that announcement officials had discussed the definition with Apatura, which is behind more Scottish data centre proposals than any other firm. Correspondence between the company and officials on the issue appears to have started at a networking drinks event at Glasgow’s plush Corinthian Club in April.”




Though the company and the government claim that Apatura’s definition has not been accepted, it is still being circulated among government officials. So far no definition has been forthcoming.




Why Scotland?




Scotland is extremely popular with developers. It has been a target for windfarms because a lot of the landscape it considered ‘empty’ with ‘nothing there’. For those whose aim is to make profits, hills and moors full of wildlife and enjoyed by people for their beauty and solitude, are nothing but places to develop. The Scottish government has also been very supportive of ‘development’. The recent conference stressed ‘growth, drilling, and data centres (

https://www.economist.com/britain/2026/10/19/the-scottish-national-party-turns-to-the-right)

.




From Tom Rampage of the Badenoch and Strathspey Herald, writing about the windfarm proposal to the west of Aviemore:




“Feel free to disagree, but it strikes us as hugely ironic that as we fear the ravaging of our landscape by global warming and assorted climate changes we appear ever keener just to do the job ourselves. There is a kind of petulance in refusing to wait for nature when we have all the weaponry we need here and now.

Having gone to all the trouble of setting up ‘the green belt’, ‘national scenic areas’, ‘sites of special scientific interest’ and the like, we can’t wait to get the diggers into them. Some sceptics believe that all these labels are stuck on our landscape as some sort of road signs for the developers.” (

https://www.facebook.com/WindEnergysAbsurd/posts/very-picturesque-isnt-it-no-wonder-that-the-house-has-been-featured-in-film-and-/1532634102227218/

)




As a result of windfarms being erected all over Scotland, the country is thought to have a strong renewable energy sector. (This claim is itself dubious as the amount of energy and minerals going in to making and transporting, and then replacing them when they wear out, detracts from the renewable credentials).




But still, accepting that wind turbines are an important part of a climate change strategy, instead of this energy going to help reduce the use of fossil fuels and give communities and local businesses a steady supply of energy, the electricity generated will be used to fuel the data centres, known for their vociferous demand.  And, during periods of low wind or when clouds are blocking the sun, it may mean having to fire up fossil fuel power stations to provide the energy required to keep the servers blinking. (

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6qxv55882z1o

)




Concerns




Many are questioning data centres. According to 

The Ferret:




“It has been estimated that if all the data centres proposed across Scotland went ahead, they would more than double the country’s demand for electricity. The industry argues they can be powered by Scotland’s growing renewable energy sector, but opponents point out they will need constant power, including when the weather means wind and solar farms are producing less, potentially increasing reliance on fossil fuels. Critics have also raised concerns about the diesel backup generators they have on site and their water requirements for cooling. As a result of these issues any description of data centres as ‘green’ is highly controversial.”




This is in addition to the massive demand for water and the impact they will have on local communities.




Demands and Resistance




The general demand seems to be for the Scottish government to introduce a moratorium to prohibit planning permission to be granted for new data centres. This call has spread across Scotland. Campaigning groups are springing up all over Scotland, and this is reflected in the rest of the UK as well as in other parts of the world.




November 14

th

 will see a demonstration in Edinburgh. Campaigners have announced a mass march against AI data centres for Edinburgh on Saturday 14

th

 November. The march is part of a Europe wide wave of protests to ‘stop dirty data centres’ with other actions in Denmark, the Netherlands, Spain, Ireland and many other countries earlier in the month. The Edinburgh protest will also coincide with a global day of action around the UN climate talks COP31 in Antalya, Turkey.




Supporters say:




 “We’re parents, neighbours and ordinary people who care about where we live and the future of Scotland. What started as a local fight for us in West Edinburgh has become a nationwide movement against US tech billionaires. We cannot allow them to dictate the future of our countryside and our communities, they do not bring the benefits that many developers, tech firms and Donald Trump would lead us to believe. We are asking the Scottish Government to stand shoulder to shoulder with us and not let this happen. Big tech, go hame tae think again!” 




Sarah Finlay, a community campaigner with West Edinburgh Against AI Data Centres




“We are marching to say that we don’t want AI data centres in Scotland. The Annan and wider Dumfries and Galloway communities have let it be known that we do not want a data centre here or anywhere else. We are calling on the Scottish Government to call in the Chapelcross data centre application, and to press the brakes on AI data centre developments across the country. The risks of these developments are numerous and serious. The health and voices of our communities matter.”




Sam Gibson, a Dumfries and Galloway resident who is campaigning against the Chapelcross AI data centre




For more information see: 




https://www.globaljustice.org.uk/event/stop-ai-data-centres-scotland-march/




https://foe.scot/press-release/thousands-expected-to-join-march-against-ai-data-centres-in-edinburgh/




Conclusion




It is great to see an anti-data centre movement developing. However, it needs to go much further than call for a moratorium on hyper data centres because it limits the scope of the campaigns. We know that capitalists are very experienced at getting around objections to planning applications by putting in more than they want, and then appearing to compromise. This could be the number and height of wind turbines, the height of tall buildings in urban areas, or the size of data centres. They will also use bribes to the local community to get their way. Making the government back down in the face of powerful Big Tech will not be easy and will take more than demos. A militant mass movement is required, one that is willing to get to the very heart of the problem- capitalism.

author: ACG
title: REBELLION IN ALBANIA
content:
On October 15, the third day of the uprising and after 138 days of peaceful daily demonstrations, the streets of Tirana were under the control of students. A small student demonstration joined the protest, demanding better educational conditions. The brutal police violence against this group turned out to be the last straw – it prompted first the students, then the rest of the population, and now high school students to speak out against police brutality and demand the resignation of the Prime Minister, the government, and the complete dismantling of their entire system.




Protesters demanding the fall of the government engaged in fierce clashes with the police. Thousands of students boycotted classes and took to the streets alongside thousands of citizens from the “Flamingo Revolution” movement to protest against a corrupt system and its primary representative, the country’s Prime Minister, Edi Rama, and demanding the latter’s resignation. He has given protected natural areas to Trump’s daughter and son-in-law, Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, for the construction of a luxury hotel complex.




During the clashes, which lasted late into the night, the buildings housing the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Economy and Finance, the Ministry of Justice, and the Constitutional Court—as well as a police station and several bank branches—were attacked and set on fire.

author: ACG
title: NON-VIOLENCE DOES NOT EXIST
content:
The text below appeared in the  journal of the Organisation Communiste Libertaire (OCL) of France, Courant Alternatif. Whilst specific French instances are referred to, we feel that this is a useful general article on the question of “non-violence.”




For ages, the debate between non-violence and violence has permeated social movements. Violence is not only physical, but also institutional, symbolic, psychological, and so on. This opposition is largely fuelled by the state. It criminalises our mobilisations by accusing them of being violent, even going so far as to accuse them of terrorism or of glorifying it. It is imperative to move beyond this opposition and try to act by taking into account and articulating the multiple forms, actions, and initiatives that social movements take.




The primary function of the state is to maintain social order: capitalist society. It is founded on exploitation, the maintenance of a social hierarchy, patriarchy, and the division of the dominated among themselves, through racialisation, the subjugation of certain genders, criminalisation, and the creation of artificial competition. All of this generates daily violent conflict. Faced with challenges to these various aspects, the state has no choice but to respond violently. author: ACG
title: Quote of the Week
content:
Parliament




Political rights do not originate in parliaments; they are, rather, forced upon parliaments from without. And even their enactment into law has for a long time been no guarantee of their security. Just as the employers always try to nullify every concession they had made to labor as soon as opportunity offered, as soon as any signs of weakness were observable in the workers’ organizations, so governments also are always inclined to restrict or to abrogate completely rights and freedoms that have been achieved if they imagine that the people will put up no resistance. Even in those countries where such things as freedom of the press, right of assembly, right of combination, and the like have long existed, governments are constantly trying to restrict those rights or to reinterpret them by juridical hair-splitting. Political rights do not exist because they have been legally set down on a piece of paper, but only when they have become the ingrown habit of a people, and when any attempt to impair them will meet with the violent resistance of the populace. Where this is not the case, there is no help in any parliamentary Opposition or any Platonic appeals to the constitution.







— Rudolf Rocker, 1947

author: ACG
title: French High School Students Rise Up
content:
From September 17

th

, high school students and staff staged blockades throughout France. This was to protest deteriorating educational conditions. The tempo of these blockades and demonstrations increased on September 29

th

 and 30

th

.




Lack of teachers, teaching assistants, special needs assistants, and nurses; poorly insulated and unrenovated facilities; and untenable class schedules… All high school students in France are suffering the consequences of insufficient funding for the national education system. This has sparked a nationwide mobilisation that is shaking the media and the government.

The national education budget has increased by 30% since 2017, so why is the situation in high schools deteriorating? For the start of the 2026 school year, approximately 4,000 teaching positions were eliminated in both public and private schools across France. Then there is Parcoursup (1) and its unfair selection system, which relies on “digital filters”. Then, in higher education, the freeze on housing benefits will prevent the most vulnerable from finding accommodation. Not to mention the “Welcome to France” decree imposed by the government before the summer, a blatantly anti-immigration project that aims to increase tuition fees for non-European international students. content:

Dossier on AI, Work in the Future Society, Age Verification, the General Strike, Mujeres Libres, and a letter from a reader on veganism. 




Editorial




Now and tomorrow




Now: Hope in Every Heart or Business as Usual?




Andy Burnham’s accession to power doesn’t mark any radical change in the direction of the Labour Party. He backs the Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood’s immigration reforms, increasing the wait for indefinite leave to remain from five years to between 10 and 20 years. He supports expanding the use of detention centres. He wrote recently in 

The Times

 that “Increasing our national security, in every sense, will be my first priority,” and that arms manufacture would be central in “regenerating and reindustrialising the country.” He threatened that he would “not be squeamish about cutting welfare” to invest more in the arms industry.




He intends to proceed with the £31bn Dreadnought-class boats and with the building of Trident nuclear submarines. He urged EU countries to supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles. author: ACG
title: When history accelerates: Maricarmen’s eviction
content:
We publish below the statement from the Spanish group Liza on the Maricarmen mobilisation and the need for revolutionary organisation.




Context: On Saturday, September 26, thousands of people marched through the streets of Madrid to protest the eviction of 87-year-old disabled  Maricarmen Abascal from her home. Her door was broken down by local riot police, and she was evicted on a stretcher despite the resistance of a cordon of protesters. Maricarmen, who had lived in her apartment for 70 years, instantly became a symbol of the housing crisis plaguing Spain, particularly in major cities. Whose fault is it? Rampant gentrification, in which real estate developers systematically buy up buildings in city centres, taking the opportunity to “revise” rents. Maricarmen’s rent, which was around 500 euros per month, was increased by 275% to 2,750 euros! Anger swept across Spain, withtens of thousands mobilised and fifty demonstrations,, particularly in Madrid, where the demonstrations, claimed as involving as high as 500,000, culminated in an impromptu encampment at Puerta del Sol, reminiscent of the 2011 protests that sparked the Indignados movement. author: ACG
title: International Conference in Varna Against War
content:
We re-publish below the statement from Konflkikt on this conference, which the ACG was unfortunately not able to attend.




From the 18th to 21st September, Konflikt organized an international conference against militarism and war.




The conference took place at a particularly turbulent time. The wars in Ukraine, Iran, Palestine, and Sudan are affecting people far beyond their borders, while nationalism, militarization, and social tensions are on the rise around the world. The working class is under attack—workers are both direct participants and victims of these wars, as well as the primary target of their economic consequences.




The near future portends further military escalation and intensified economic attacks. However, it may also lead to a strengthening of class resistance against war, economic crises, and the international capitalist system that gives rise to them.




That is why, this September, we brought together internationalists from various organizations in Bulgaria, Greece, Cyprus, Hungary, Germany, England, Poland, Italy, Croatia, and Ireland to speak openly, exchange experiences, and build stronger ties. Representatives from the International Workers’ Association (IWA) and Internationalist Communist Tendency (ICT) also attended the meeting. In addition to Konflikt, Bulgarian organizations that participated included the Federation of Anarcho-Communists in
